summary: For ages 5–6, teach the PURPOSE of weather forecasting and severe-weather preparedness (not forecasting technique). Land two ideas: (1) a forecast tells us what the weather will PROBABLY do so we can PLAN (grab a coat, cancel a trip); (2) for severe weather (storm, flood, heat, blizzard) forecasts warn us so we can prepare and stay safe. Drive learning through the child's OWN questions ('why do we watch the weather?', 'what do we do if a big storm is coming?'), the Asking-Questions practice at the heart of this topic. The strongest route at this age enacts the forecast→decision→consequence loop so purpose is felt, not merely told; preparation matching and an in-role forecaster interview complement it; recognition checks verify the evidence targets. Keep 'how forecasts are made' light (scientists watch and measure the sky) and defer satellites/radar/models to a later 7–9 topic. Prerequisite: Seasonal changes.
misconceptions: 'The forecast/weather person MAKES the weather happen' — they predict and report it, they don't control it.
'A forecast is always exactly right' — it's a good prediction, not a guarantee; sometimes it changes.
'Severe weather is nothing to prepare for / always a disaster' — balance: storms can be serious, but preparing keeps us safe (reassurance).
'Checking the weather is just for fun' — its purpose is planning and safety.
'Weather and climate/season are the same' — a forecast is about the next day or two, not the whole season.

activities.title: Plan the day from the forecast
steps: Look at a simple forecast card (today/tomorrow with weather icons) that shows, e.g., heavy rain.
Decide what the character should grab or do before going out (just a t-shirt, or a coat and umbrella).
See the consequence play out: sent out coatless in the rain, the character comes back soaked and shivering; given a coat and umbrella, they stay dry and happy.
Repeat with a scorching-sun forecast (right call: sun hat, water, shade) and with a storm warning (safe call: stay indoors).
Each round, say in your own words WHY the forecast mattered — it let you get ready.
activities.insight: A forecast's purpose is seen in the action it prompts: knowing what the weather will probably do lets us prepare so the day goes well and we stay safe.

activities.title: Get-ready matching for severe weather
steps: Match each severe-weather warning (storm, flood, heat wave, blizzard) to a sensible, calm preparation.
For at least two of these, say aloud one thing people do to stay safe and why.
Talk about a real routine you know that fits (a snow day closing school, a wet-play day, a sun-cream day).
activities.insight: Different severe weather calls for different, simple preparations; forecasts warn us ahead of time so communities can get ready and stay safe.

activities.title: Interview the weather presenter
steps: Post your own weather questions on a question board, e.g. 'why do people check the weather?', 'what should we do if a storm is coming?'
Ask a friendly weather-presenter character (a grown-up in role, or a classroom puppet/persona) your questions.
Listen to short, reassuring answers in role and ask a follow-up ('what if the forecast is wrong?').
Find and share one answer together from a sensible source.
activities.insight: Scientists forecast the weather so people can plan and stay safe; asking good questions and finding answers is how we learn about weather and hazards.

activities.title: Why do we check the forecast? (purpose check)
steps: Answer 'why do we check the weather forecast?' choosing from options (e.g. to plan and stay safe; just for fun; to make the weather happen).
Match a forecast to the preparation it should prompt.
Talk about this: 'The TV forecast said it will probably rain tomorrow. A child says the forecaster is making it rain. Is that right? What does a forecast actually do, and why is it useful?'
Say what you would do if the forecast said sun but it rained.
activities.insight: A forecaster predicts (not controls) the likely weather from clues; a forecast is a good prediction, not a guarantee, and its purpose is to help people plan and stay safe.

checkQuestion: The weather forecast on TV said it will probably rain tomorrow. A child says, 'So the weather forecaster is making it rain tomorrow.' Is that right? What does a weather forecast actually do, and why is it useful?
checkAnswer: No — the forecaster doesn't make the weather. They study clues, like the clouds and their measurements, to work out what the weather will PROBABLY do, and tell us ahead of time. It's useful because we can plan and stay safe — take a coat, or stay indoors in a storm.
